sentences.text: Sleep came up the hill from the bottom, and it took about ninety minutes to get to the top, and everybody in Casal do Meio knew their own place in the order.
The bottom houses got it first.

That was the tannery row, along the stream, six houses in a line with damp walls and the best sleep in the district — children down by half eight, adults gone by ten, nobody in that row awake past eleven for as long as anybody could remember.
Then the middle: the square, the shop, the six or seven houses behind the church.
Then the terrace on the bend.
Then the four houses at the top, where Duarte lived, which got it last, and which had got it last since before his grandmother was born.
The top houses were a joke in that village and had been for generations.
Anybody at the top who complained about being tired was told they had brought it on themselves by living up there, which made no sense and was said with great satisfaction.

There was a rhyme about it that Duarte's grandmother knew four lines of and that nobody knew the rest of, and there was a thing the tannery row said about the top houses at weddings, and there was a particular way of saying *ah, you're from the top* that had been in use in that village since at least the 1930s.
None of it was unkind.
All of it was extremely tiresome if you happened to be twelve and living in one of the four.
Duarte had never much minded until he was twelve, when he started at the school in the town and had to be at the bus at ten past seven.
Ninety minutes is nothing when you are nine and there is no bus.

Ninety minutes is a considerable amount of your life when you are getting up at a quarter past six five days a week, and Duarte spent the whole of that autumn doing an arithmetic that had never occurred to anybody in his family: that over a school year the top of the hill loses something in the region of two hundred and seventy hours to the bottom of it.
He put this to his mother, who said that was very interesting and asked whether he had done his Portuguese.
The donkey came up at about half past eight.
You did not have to watch for her.
Everybody in Casal do Meio has seen her at some point, usually by accident, usually from a window, and the thing they all say is the same: she is entirely ordinary.
She is a small grey donkey with a dark cross on her shoulders and one ear that goes sideways, and she comes up the road at a walk, and she is carrying two panniers, and the panniers are full.
Full of what is not a question anybody in that village asks, and Duarte had learned by about six that asking got you a look.

He had got the look from four different adults by the time he was eight and had eventually stopped, and the interesting thing — the thing he only understood as a grown man — is that the look was not disapproval.
It was embarrassment.
Nobody knew, and nobody had ever known, and a village does not enjoy being asked a question about a thing it has lived beside for two hundred years without ever once looking into.
She goes up the road and turns in at the tannery row first and stands in the middle of it for a bit.
Then the square.
Then the terrace.
Then, last, up the track to the four houses at the top, where she arrives at about ten o'clock, and after that the whole village is asleep and the road is empty.
